title: Beyond roguelikes
thesis: The roguelike's core machinery (runs, permanent loss, generated variety inside a fixed container) is portable: talks find it in novels, reality TV, card drafting and classrooms, graft it onto city builders, platformers and gardening games, and carry it onto paper, into rooms, onto 3D printers and into podcasts. Each move teaches something about the original: which element is doing the work, what a human referee or a physical object does better than a computer, and when a generator should provoke a person rather than finish the job. A designer should leave able to name the structural element they are borrowing or exporting, and to adapt it to the new medium's constraints instead of copying its surface.

sections.heading: The roguelike lens: runs and permadeath in other forms
sections.brief: Argue that roguelike structure (repeated runs, permanent loss, a fixed container filled with variable content) is recognisable well outside videogames, and that reading other forms through this lens is a source of design ideas to steal back. Lead with the strongest cases: Younès Rabii reading La Horde du Contrevent as a roguelike through mechanics, interface and narration, Florence Smith Nicholls on Love Island's recoupling as a new run and dumping as permadeath, Gavin Verhey on Magic draft as a multiplayer run (and all of Magic as one branching roguelike), and Stella Vermilion's Nuzlocke, a player-imposed permadeath ruleset on Pokemon that she argues roguelikes could learn from. Converge these with Dennis Greger's reading of Survivor as a 'procedural container' and his 'fly in the soup' sifting loop, Britta's fan fiction as a tag-driven generator, Joel Clark on sports as simple rules producing chaos, and Matthew Henderson's poetry collection that uses runs and permanent death to work through grief. Then the applied end: Gillian Smith's WPI as a roguelike of risk-taking without failing grades and her 'caramelized cauliflower' rule against points-and-badges gamification, Nat Alison's teaching of maths as discovery, Stephen Ware's deterministic, replayable VR trainer, and Salzman's low-commitment Dynasty Warriors. Close with Zapata's note that the influence now runs both ways and give guidance: when you borrow from another form, name the structural element (the run, the container, the loss) you are taking, not its surface.

sections.heading: Grafting the roguelike onto other genres, formats and platforms
sections.brief: How do you combine roguelike structure with another genre without one swallowing the other? Open with method: Jonathan Lessard and Pippin Barr's Chogue rule that every element must come from chess or Rogue, which turns an infinite design space into a mappable one, and Tyriq Plummer's argument that genres whose defining features barely overlap (roguelike and platformer) force invention, while Vagante and Catacomb Kids show that which mechanics you borrow matters more than proportion. Then the main pattern several talks converge on: distil the target genre's best loop into a run, as Against the Storm did with a city builder's first two hours, Legends of Runeterra did to restore power progression, and card roguelikes do by making cards stand for spells, gear and encounters (Benjamin Berman; Alexander King on the pick-one-of-three default and the untried set-based alternative; Meteorfall's swipe method). Set against it translation that changes the source genre's feel: Josh Grams making inertial space flight turn-based so players can experiment, Brian Walker freezing time in a platformer to keep it cerebral, Bruno Dias and Nicholas Feinberg on how space sims and Civilization II reward routine over discovery, Nic Tringali cutting board-game planning time in The Banished Vault, Oath borrowing from Caves of Qud, Todd Furmanski revisiting Myst. Then format and platform: MIT Mystery Hunt roguelike puzzles (WASD, mirrored control, answer extraction), mobile ADOM as a separate variant, smartwatch and VR roguelikes, Lee Tusman's one-dimensional dungeons, Zeno Rogue on rectangles needing Euclid. End with practical guidance: decide what each parent genre contributes, constrain the source pool, and expect a new platform to need a simplified variant rather than a port.

sections.heading: New verbs and new subjects: non-violent, cozy and everyday roguelikes
sections.brief: Ask what replaces killing and looting when you change the subject of a roguelike. Lead with Tabea Iseli's Grimoire Groves, which keeps the roguelite crawler loop but maps every violent element to growing plants, gathering fruit and energy, and is candid about what did not map (why would a plant boss block progress?); pair with her point that farming and roguelites share resource collection, player-chosen priorities and goals across runs. Then Max Kreminski's 'gardening' as a mode of play (nurturing a system you guide but do not control, plus customisation), his Epitaph example, and his unresolved boundary with 'farming' games that extract value; set Salzman's Animal Crossing (drop any task without penalty) beside it. Show other ways to find fresh material: Ludipe's list of everyday themes (cooking, laundry, trip planning), Philomena Schwab's search for familiar real-world mechanics after Peglin (Dungeon Clawler's claw machine), Boyfriend Dungeon fusing dating and combat, Nick Bush reading Vi and Emacs commands as roguelike verbs, and the empathy-not-conquest history game. End with guidance: map each loop element explicitly to the new theme, find where the mapping breaks, and look in ordinary activities and tools for verbs.

sections.heading: Roguelikes on paper and at the table
sections.brief: Argue that the roguelike's machinery (lookup tables, dice, hidden state, generated content) translates to paper and board games, and that the table offers things in return. Lead with Francesco Cottone's Chronicles of Stampadia, a daily one-page print-and-play roguelike, and his framing of single-sheet puzzle games as a platform; then his sources: Four Against Darkness generating dungeons from dice tables, Fabled Lands storing secret state in checkboxes, exploration board games, and his claim that story-driven board games need random generation because table stories must be short. Set Cole Wehrle's Oath (players as the best generator, piping their invented history back into the game) and Cezar Capacle's GM-less 'anti-canon' RPGs against designer-authored content. Then human versus computer referee: Jason Grinblat on how tabletop frames fail gracefully because people negotiate them, Jon Perry on tabletop's freeing limits, and Berman on effects a computer does better but which can be prototyped on paper. Close with tools: Atty Vohra's D&D encounter generator and advice to automate the parts of GMing you find tedious, Phenry Ewing's Monte Carlo balancing of Werewolf, Tringali's Wheel to Wheel and Tall Ships, and economic board games as a source (Robin Mendoza). End with practical guidance on moving state, randomness and bookkeeping off the computer.

sections.heading: Many players, crowds and audiences
sections.brief: What happens to roguelike design when more than one person plays? Open with the two visions: the Delve Bros' Stream Heist as 'infinite multiplayer' for a streamer's whole audience, and Leif Bloomquist's Dungeon of the Rogue Daemon, where the other characters in the dungeon are players who share tools and clues. Set the problems they converge on: griefing and trolling (Bloomquist's teleporting key, the Delve Bros treating trolling as part of the fun), scale (a hundred viewers versus eight friends; a crowd-scaled puzzle where each person's success is chance) and their proposed fixes (varied mini-games, shared progress, multi-part devices), plus Bloomquist's emergent party roles from a two-item inventory. Add Joe Sondow's Twitter games (polls as four-option choices, first reply moves, inclusion as the goal), Stella Mazeika's randomizers and multiworld item sharing, and the Dungeon Court live format. Set Verhey's wish for more co-op against his point that endless replay makes single-player critical. End with guidance: design for griefing from the start, make each participant's contribution visible, and choose one audience scale.

sections.heading: Play in rooms, bodies and real software
sections.brief: Argue that physical space and the player's body can carry the variety and personal discovery that roguelikes usually generate. Lead with Emilia Lazer-Walker's Sleep No More, deterministic 'clockwork' with a possibility space so large every visitor finds private moments, then Janet Cardiff's fixed audio walk that feels personal because it leans on reliable real-world events, and Computational Flaneur's location-seeded poetry. Then G blekkenhorst's interface games (the player in front of software the characters could have used; metaleptic games that never break that fiction; tangible versions in a room) and their warning that once players are on the computer they stop noticing the room; contrast Paris Buttfield-Addison's Hintline 93, whose paper binder deliberately pulls attention off the screen. Add live forms: Bad News's death notification with an actor and Dustin Freeman's live-action roguelike with sets rebuilt between levels. End with the cost of physical commitment (You Are a Strange Sensor's kneeling posture excluded people) and guidance on where to put information so players use the space.

sections.heading: Generating things you can hold: fabrication and keepsakes
sections.brief: What changes when a generator's output is a physical object? Lead with Adrian Herbez's Plarl, whose goals (single-player, procedural, hidden information, printing integral not incidental) produced a dungeon you break open door by door, and his 'design for failure' tolerances; bleeptrack's warning that manufacturing works against variety and her middle path for PCBs; and Ada Null's point that how viewers encounter the output (Kiss Garden's endless receipt) carries meaning. Then Florence Smith Nicholls on keepsake games, play that produces a memorable artifact, using existing generators as prompts (Watabou's city generator, tarot cards for archive artifacts). Close with technique: vector output for plotters, hand-assembled paper lanterns, rubber-stamp tiles that let people run the generator by hand, Herbez's greeble modeler, and Plarl's theatre-of-the-mind gap. End with guidance on matching generator output to the fabrication method and budget.

sections.heading: The generator as partner, prompt and living work
sections.brief: Argue that outside games a generator's job is often to change what a human does, not to produce finished work, so the bar is low and small amounts of randomness go far. Lead with Clarissa Littler's poetry generator that produces shapes of poems and her claim that a creative partner only needs to make you write differently; converge with Max Hawkins submitting to random choices to escape preference loops (and randomness as a step before curation), Nick Montfort treating generated text as material, Botnik's source-specific predictive text, Chelsea Thompto's 'single drop of randomization' and designing relationships rather than narrative, and Sol LeWitt's instruction-based wall drawings (Mark Gritter). Set Nat Alison's case for hand-crafted variant sudoku, where human rule invention beats generated grids, against this, alongside droqen's sudoku poems. Then works that keep generating: Neutrinowatch's daily-regenerated podcast (self-similar like a set list, live data felt rather than charted), Sondow's Tiny Star Fields, Kate Compton's Chancery chatbots, Diarytown's malleable simulation, and the Xenotext's bacterial generator and slime molds as biological ones. Close with Cedotal's careers as skill combos and Alison's Fibonacci plots. End with guidance: decide whether your generator is meant to finish the work or provoke a person, and size it accordingly.
